newsitem.title: MEXICO: Rebels, crime hurt U.S. investment in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Rebels, crime hurt U.S. investment in Mexico.

text.p: Concern about kidnappings, guerrilla groups and other crime has led U.S. investment in Mexico to slow down in the second half of this year, American ambassador James Jones said in an interview.
"There's a great deal of enthusiasm for investment and during the first half of the year we thought it was going to be a record year for foreign direct investment," Jones said on Friday.
"But from the mid-year forward there has been a reticence to actually make the investment therefore it's not going to be a record year."
Battered by a deep recession last year which cost over a million jobs, Mexico's economy is recovering slowly. Most economists expect 4 percent growth this year, after a 6.2 percent decline last year.
But fragile confidence abroad in Mexico took a knock at the end of June when a new Marxist guerrilla group, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), unexpectedly appeared.
August was a particularly bad month for Mexico in the world's news headlines.

The president of a U.S. subsidiary of Japan's Sanyo Electric Co. was kidnapped in the northern border city of Tijuana and the EPR launched a coordinated wave of surprise attacks in four states, killing 15 people.
Some private security firms have said they consider Mexico a kidnapping trouble spot in the region, along with Colombia and Brazil.

Jones said U.S. executives considering investment in Mexico "raise questions about the kidnappings, groups like the EPR, narcotrafficking. They raise questions about how serious it is, how secure is it, they want to sort those issues out."
Mexican government figures for direct foreign investment have been sporadic of late.

The latest government figures for foreign direct investment, released in August, showed investment in the first half of this year of $1.50 billion had been registered. No comparative figure was given for the first half of last year.

Jones said there was still a great deal of interest from U.S. companies in investing in Mexico and predicted that as the economic recovery gathered steam and started affecting more average Mexicans "that will change a tremendous amount of attitudes."
